prompt: A hypothetical open-pit gold project reports Mineral Resources under the JORC Code (2012) at a 0.5 g/t Au cut-off, stated 'inclusive of Ore Reserves': Measured 6.0 Mt at 1.80 g/t, Indicated 14.0 Mt at 1.40 g/t and Inferred 9.0 Mt at 1.10 g/t. The separate Ore Reserve statement shows Proved 4.5 Mt at 1.70 g/t and Probable 7.5 Mt at 1.30 g/t, both after dilution and measured at the plant feed. An investor slide headed 'Total project inventory' adds the Reserve tonnes to the Resource tonnes and quotes one combined figure. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. (a) Calculate the contained gold in the Measured plus Indicated Resource, in thousand ounces. (b) Calculate the contained gold in the Ore Reserve, in thousand ounces. (c) Express (b) as a percentage of (a). (d) State whether the slide is acceptable and how the two statements should be presented.
reference_answer: (a) Measured 6.0 Mt x 1.80 g/t = 10.8 t Au; Indicated 14.0 Mt x 1.40 g/t = 19.6 t Au; together 30.4 t = 30.4e6 g / 31.1035 = 977.4 koz. (b) Proved 4.5 x 1.70 = 7.65 t; Probable 7.5 x 1.30 = 9.75 t; together 17.4 t = 559.4 koz. (c) 559.4 / 977.4 = 57.2%. So roughly 57% of the Measured and Indicated gold has been carried into the Ore Reserve (the comparison is approximate, because Reserve tonnes and grade include dilution and losses that the Resource does not). (d) The slide is not acceptable. The Resources are stated inclusive of Ore Reserves, so the Reserve material is already inside the Measured and Indicated figures; adding Reserve tonnes to Resource tonnes counts that material twice. The Code states that Ore Reserve estimates must not be aggregated with Mineral Resource estimates to report a single combined figure. The Inferred 9.0 Mt is also not Reserve material and must not be blended into an 'inventory' with higher-confidence categories without showing each category separately. Correct presentation: a Resource table by category with the clarifying statement that it is inclusive of Reserves, a separate Reserve table by Proved and Probable, and a comment that Reserve tonnes and grade include dilution so the two tables are not directly comparable.

rubric.criterion: States that Ore Reserve estimates must not be aggregated with Mineral Resource estimates into a single combined figure.
Recognises that, because the Resource is stated inclusive of Ore Reserves, adding Reserve tonnes to Resource tonnes double counts the Reserve material.
Notes that Inferred Resources are not part of the Reserve and should not be folded into a combined 'inventory' figure with Measured and Indicated.
Notes that Reserve tonnes and grade include dilution and losses, so Resource and Reserve tables are not directly comparable and the difference should be explained.
Recommends separate Resource and Reserve tables with an explicit inclusive/additional clarifying statement.

sources.citation: JORC Code 2012 edition: clauses 34 and 36 (reporting of Ore Reserves; clarifying inclusive/additional statement; no aggregation of Reserve with Resource; Inferred generally additional to Reserves except as dilution) (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)

review_notes: Trap: adding Reserve to Resource double counts when the Resource is inclusive. The 57% is a deliberately approximate comparison (the Reserve includes dilution); part (c) is a simple ratio of contained gold and the reference says so. Cl 36 verified against the PDF. Whether the grader accepts a 'total' for an exclusive-basis statement is out of scope for this item. Reviewer: JORC clauses 34 and 36 checked against the PDF text; arithmetic passes.

prompt: A hypothetical pre-feasibility study (PFS) for an orogenic gold project, reported under NI 43-101 and the CIM Definition Standards, schedules a 14.0 Mt life-of-mine plant feed: 9.1 Mt of Indicated Mineral Resource (diluted, 2.10 g/t Au) and 4.9 Mt of Inferred Mineral Resource (diluted, 1.50 g/t Au). Plant gold recovery is 92%. The company announces an 'Ore Reserve' of 14.0 Mt at 1.89 g/t and a PFS NPV, saying the Inferred part 'is low-risk because it lies in the same lode and is mostly sitting inside the planned pit'. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. (a) What percentage of the plan tonnes and (b) what percentage of the plan's contained gold is Inferred? (c) How many thousand ounces of recovered gold come from the Inferred part? (d) Assess the announcement, and say what a defensible Reserve and economic statement would look like.
reference_answer: (a) 4.9 / 14.0 = 35.0% of plan tonnes. (b) Contained gold: Indicated 9.1 Mt x 2.10 = 19.11 t; Inferred 4.9 Mt x 1.50 = 7.35 t; Inferred share = 7.35 / 26.46 = 27.8%. (c) Inferred recovered gold = 7.35 t x 0.92 = 6.762 t = 6.762e6 / 31.1035 = 217.4 koz. (d) The announcement is not acceptable. A Mineral Reserve is the economically mineable part of a Measured and/or Indicated Mineral Resource; an Inferred Mineral Resource must not be converted to a Reserve (definition), and the CIM guidance to that definition states that Inferred material must not be included in the economic analysis, production schedule or mine life of a publicly disclosed pre-feasibility or feasibility study. The statement that the Inferred portion is 'low-risk' because it lies in the same lode misses the point: Inferred confidence is, by definition, too low for the application of Modifying Factors. Defensible version: declare a Probable Ore Reserve only from the Indicated part (at most 9.1 Mt, 65% of the plan tonnes, and less once the pit and schedule are re-run without the Inferred material; the mine life shortens and the NPV falls). Any Inferred-supported case belongs in a preliminary economic assessment with the Inferred proportion and sequencing disclosed and the required cautionary statements, not in a PFS Reserve or headline NPV.

rubric.criterion: States that an Inferred Mineral Resource must not be converted to a Mineral (Ore) Reserve, so the declared 14.0 Mt Reserve is overstated by the Inferred tonnes.
States that Inferred material must not be included in the economic analysis, production schedule or mine life of a publicly disclosed PFS/FS (CIM guidance).
Identifies that only the Indicated 9.1 Mt (and any Measured) can support a Probable Reserve.
Rejects the 'same lode, low-risk' argument on the grounds that Inferred confidence is too low to apply Modifying Factors in detail.
Says that an Inferred-supported case belongs in a preliminary economic assessment/scoping-level study with proportion and sequencing disclosed and cautionary language, not in a PFS headline NPV.

sources.citation: CIM Definition Standards for Mineral Resources and Mineral Reserves (2014): definition of Inferred Mineral Resource (must not be converted to a Mineral Reserve) and its italic guidance (must not be included in the economic analysis, production schedules or mine life of publicly disclosed pre-feasibility or feasibility studies), p. 4-5; Mineral Reserve definition, p. 6 (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)

JORC Code 2012 edition: clauses 21, 29 and 38 (Inferred must not be converted to Ore Reserve; Ore Reserve is the economically mineable part of a Measured and/or Indicated Mineral Resource; Scoping Study use of Inferred with proportion and cautionary statement) (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)
National Instrument 43-101 Standards of Disclosure for Mineral Projects, provisions on Inferred Mineral Resources in preliminary economic assessments (section numbers not checked)

review_notes: Trap: the headline reserve blends 35% Inferred tonnes; fluent answers just say 'high risk' without stating that Inferred cannot be in a PFS/FS plan at all. Jurisdiction is NI 43-101/CIM so the CIM wording is the controlling cite; JORC clauses given as parallel. NI 43-101 PEA rule cited by topic only (unverified). 'Probable Reserve from Indicated only' is stated as the principle; exact reserve size needs re-optimisation. Reviewer: JORC clauses 21, 29, 38 checked against the PDF text; CIM wording not re-opened.

prompt: A hypothetical alluvial gold project on a river terrace in West Africa, reporting under the JORC Code (2012), estimates a gravel resource from pitting. Reported in-situ (bank, undisturbed) grade is 0.32 g/m3 at a 0.15 g/m3 cut-off, on a gravel volume of 21.0 million bank m3. The resource table converts to tonnes using 2.4 t/m3, taken from a laboratory measurement on competent quartzite pebbles, and converts grade to g/t using the field-weighed in-situ wet bulk density of 1.85 t/m3 (0.32 / 1.85 = 0.173 g/t). The table therefore states 50.4 Mt at 0.173 g/t. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. (a) Calculate the contained gold, in thousand ounces, directly from volume and g/m3 grade. (b) Calculate the contained gold implied by the table's 50.4 Mt at 0.173 g/t, using 0.32/1.85 g/t without further rounding. (c) State the difference between (b) and (a), as a percentage of (a). (d) Assess the resource table's conversion, and comment on the Competent Person experience needed to sign off an alluvial gold estimate.
reference_answer: (a) 21.0e6 m3 x 0.32 g/m3 = 6.72 t = 6.72e6 / 31.1035 = 216.1 koz. (b) 21.0e6 x 2.4 = 50.4 Mt; grade 0.32/1.85 = 0.17297 g/t; contained = 50.4e6 x 0.17297 = 8.718 t = 280.3 koz. (c) 280.3 / 216.1 - 1 = 29.7%, which equals 2.4/1.85 - 1. (d) The tonnage and the grade were converted with two different densities, so the density factor does not cancel as it should and metal is inflated by 2.4/1.85 = 1.297. A grade measured per bank cubic metre must be combined with the bank volume, or both tonnes and g/t must use the same in-situ density. The 2.4 t/m3 pebble value is a grain density of the clasts, not the in-situ bulk density of gravel with voids and moisture. Density is part of what must be estimated with sufficient confidence for Indicated or Measured classification, and the moisture basis (wet or dry) must be stated. The error does not touch the g/m3 route, which is why reporting volume and g/m3 is often cleaner for alluvials. On the person: the JORC Code requires a Competent Person with at least five years' relevant experience in the style of mineralisation and the activity; its guidance gives alluvial gold as an example where considerable experience in the evaluation and extraction of that type is needed and placer experience with other minerals does not automatically transfer.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that tonnes were computed with 2.4 t/m3 but grade converted with 1.85 t/m3, so the density does not cancel and contained metal is overstated.
States that contained gold should equal volume x g/m3 (about 216 koz) independent of density, or that both conversions must use the same in-situ density.
Explains that the 2.4 t/m3 laboratory pebble value is not an in-situ bulk density, and that the moisture basis must be stated.
Notes that densities must be estimated with sufficient confidence for Indicated/Measured categories.
Notes that Competent Person relevant experience for alluvial gold needs alluvial/placer gold experience (five-year minimum in the relevant style and activity).

sources.citation: JORC Code 2012 edition: clauses 22 and 23 (Indicated and Measured definitions include densities); clause 11 and its guidance on relevant experience, including alluvial gold example (guidance text, not a rule) (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)

review_notes: Trap: a density factor applied twice with different values. Everything is arithmetic and checkable. The CP paragraph rests on italic guidance in cl 11 (the five-year minimum is in the bold definition; the alluvial example is guidance), so it carries a low weight. Reviewer may prefer a higher-difficulty variant with wet/dry moisture; kept at 2 on purpose. Reviewer: JORC clauses 11, 22, 23 checked against the PDF text (density in the Indicated and Measured definitions).

prompt: A hypothetical open-pit gold project reports, under the JORC Code (2012), Indicated plus Inferred Mineral Resources of 62 Mt at 0.62 g/t Au at a 0.30 g/t cut-off, taken from every block inside a geological wireframe down to 520 m below surface, with no pit optimisation shell. The reasonable-prospects section lists: gold price US$2,000/oz, recovery 88%, royalty 5% of recovered-gold revenue, mining US$4.00/t (per tonne of plant feed, including waste handling), processing US$14.00/t and G&A US$2.30/t. A scoping-level pit optimisation shell using these same price and costs reaches 260 m depth and contains 31 Mt at 0.74 g/t; the remaining 31 Mt of the reported resource lies outside that shell. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. Define the marginal cut-off as (processing + G&A)/(net revenue per g/t) and the full-cost cut-off as (mining + processing + G&A)/(net revenue per g/t), where net revenue per g/t of plant feed = price per gram x recovery x (1 - royalty). (a) Calculate the marginal cut-off. (b) Calculate the full-cost cut-off. (c) Calculate the thousand ounces of contained gold in the reported resource that lie outside the optimised shell. (d) Assess whether the resource statement meets the reasonable-prospects requirement and what the Competent Person should do.
reference_answer: Net revenue per g/t of plant feed = 2,000/31.1035 x 0.88 x 0.95 = US$53.76. (a) Marginal cut-off = (14.00 + 2.30)/53.76 = 0.303 g/t, which is the stated 0.30 g/t. (b) Full-cost cut-off = 20.30/53.76 = 0.378 g/t. (c) Reported contained gold = 62 x 0.62 = 38.44 t; inside shell 31 x 0.74 = 22.94 t; outside = 15.50 t = 498 koz, about 40% of the reported metal. (d) The statement does not demonstrate reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. The reported cut-off is the marginal (mill-feed) cut-off, which is valid only for material that would be mined anyway; applied to every block in a wireframe it ignores the mining cost of getting deep material out and the strip ratio. The Code says portions of a deposit without reasonable prospects must not be included, that a Mineral Resource is not an inventory of all mineralisation drilled regardless of cut-off or likely mining dimensions, and that cut-off grades should be realistic for the style of mineralisation and the anticipated mining and processing options. The CP should constrain the statement with an optimisation shell (or underground stope shapes) at a justified price, report only material inside it, and disclose the basis. If deeper material is to be retained, the CP must justify a credible underground or deeper-pit case; the 31 Mt below 260 m (about 40% of the gold) cannot be reported on the strength of a marginal cut-off alone.

rubric.criterion: States that the resource is unconstrained (no pit optimisation shell or equivalent mining constraint) so material without reasonable prospects of eventual economic extraction is included.
Identifies the reported 0.30 g/t as the marginal (processing + G&A) cut-off, not a full-cost breakeven that includes mining.
Concludes that about 31 Mt and about 498 koz (about 40% of the reported metal) lie outside the economic shell and should be removed or separately justified.
Recommends constraining by a shell or stope optimisation at justified assumptions, disclosing the basis, or giving a credible alternative (underground) case for the deeper material.
Does not treat higher confidence category or a clean drilling database as a substitute for reasonable prospects.

sources.citation: JORC Code 2012 edition: clause 20 (reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction; portions without reasonable prospects must not be included; guidance that a Mineral Resource is not an inventory of all mineralisation drilled) and clause 24 guidance (cut-off grades realistic in relation to style of mineralisation and anticipated mining and processing) (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)

CIM Definition Standards for Mineral Resources and Mineral Reserves (2014): Mineral Resource definition and guidance on reasonable prospects (assumptions to include cut-off grade, recovery, price, mining and processing costs), p. 4 (retrieved 21 Nov 2026)

review_notes: Trap: the quoted cut-off equals the marginal value, so a fluent answer calls it 'consistent' and misses the missing shell. Judgement call: the grader should accept an answer that says deeper material could be retained only with a justified underground case; the reference does not say all 31 Mt must be removed. Mining cost per tonne of feed is a stated simplification (no separate strip ratio). Reviewer: JORC clauses 20 and 24 checked against the PDF text. Outside-shell material averages 0.50 g/t, above the 0.38 full-cost cut-off, so the case against it rests on depth and strip, which is why the rubric accepts a justified underground case.
